transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Time: 15:00 PDT (58 minutes)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Javier Morales (Orion HoML), Priya Singh (SRE), Daniel Park (CTO)

Summary: quick check-in on the pilot — focus on gating rules for autoscale, prewarming for bursts, and fallback behavior when Dedicated capacity hits limits.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Javier Morales: Javier here.
[00:09] Priya Singh: Priya here.
[00:11] Daniel Park: Daniel here.
[00:13] Maya Chen: Great, Ethan from our side?
[00:16] Ethan Cole: Yep, Ethan here.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Cool, so objective today — traffic shaping and fallback rules, make sure the policies we're running in the Dedicated pilot are protecting your SLAs while keeping costs predictable.

[02:05] Javier Morales: Quick context — last week's run we saw a ~2.8x spike on our weekend window, average tokens per request stayed around 420 but tails went up to 1.2K, and the KV cache hit was about 22% which surprised us, we thought the prefix cache would be higher.
[02:28] Ethan Cole: Mm-hmm. We looked at the traces you shared, the batching window was at 20ms which helps throughput but pushed some requests into higher latency under that burst. Also saw a few cold starts on new replicas when concurrency crossed the threshold.
[02:45] Priya Singh: Those cold starts are painful for us — they show up as 500ms+ tails and trigger pager alerts. We want to avoid that during the 3-hour weekend window.

[04:10] Maya Chen: Right. Two levers we've surfaced are: 1) gating by target_latency instead of pure concurrency and 2) prewarm triggers based on predicted traffic using the burst profile. Idea is to keep tail latency under your SLO while limiting max replicas to control cost.
[04:34] Daniel Park: Can you explain gating by target_latency? Is that a Redwood thing or something we can export to k8s?
[04:44] Ethan Cole: It's implemented in our autoscaler. Instead of scaling when active connections exceed N, it observes p95 latency over a sliding window — if p95 > target_latency for two consecutive windows, we open a scale-up gate. Conversely, for scale-down we require sustained p50 below a lower threshold. You could model this in k8s HPA with custom metrics, but our runtime has tighter hooks into KV cache and batching so it's more efficient.
[05:12] Javier Morales: Okay that makes sense. What's the typical window we should use?
[05:18] Ethan Cole: We usually recommend 30s windows with two-window confirmation for upscales, so about 60s to react. For your traffic shape — short spikes — we can also use a burst_capacity token bucket to allow short overages without immediately spinning replicas.
[05:36] Priya Singh: Burst token bucket — so that lets extra requests land on existing replicas until tokens are exhausted?
[05:40] Ethan Cole: Exactly. You can think of it as leaky bucket; it smooths short bursts. Then prewarm policies kick in if predictive models indicate a sustained elevation.

[07:02] Maya Chen: We proposed in the model YAML: target_latency = 120ms (p95), max_replicas = 12, burst_capacity = 3x baseline, and prewarm threshold at 1.5x for 5 minutes. That's conservative but keeps your tails under control.
[07:25] Javier Morales: 12 replicas seems high — our cost team flagged that. Can we do dynamic max depending on region? Our EU region has lower budget.
[07:33] Ethan Cole: You can set per-region max_replicas. Also can use a cheaper quantized model variant as fallback when capacity would exceed region max. That saves cost while still returning responses.
[07:48] Daniel Park: Fallback to smaller model — what's the user-visible effect? Latency change? Quality drop?
[07:54] Ethan Cole: Latency generally improves (smaller model), but there may be measurable quality regression on long-form summarization cases. We recommend running canary evals on a holdout prompt set to measure acceptable degradation.
[08:09] Priya Singh: On security — if we failover regionally, do logs and audit trails cross borders? We have data residency concerns for EU.
[08:18] Maya Chen: Good call. Our cross-region failover can be configured to respect residency: either failover only within the same compliance region, or send redacted payloads to secondary regions. We also stream audit logs to your KMS/HSM endpoint and maintain retention that you configure.
[08:39] Javier Morales: Would that impact latency when doing the redaction?
[08:43] Ethan Cole: Slightly, yes, but we can do redaction asynchronously for some telemetry; the inference path remains minimal.

[10:00] Daniel Park: Back to autoscale — what's the cold start mitigation you mentioned? Prewarming replicas or caching kernels?
[10:08] Ethan Cole: Both. We prewarm by loading weights and JIT kernels; we also keep a small hot pool on standby (1-2 warm replicas) during predicted windows. Kernel cache warmup reduces first-token penalty substantially.
[10:22] Maya Chen: For your weekend 3x spike, we recommend a rehearsal: increase prewarm to 2x and run a controlled load for 40 minutes to validate cold starts don't exceed the 150ms tail.
[10:34] Priya Singh: We'll do that test but need the exact steps and the YAML we should apply.
[10:38] Maya Chen: I'll send the policy YAML with comments and a short runbook.

[12:40] Javier Morales: About prefix/KV cache — we expected higher cache hit. Any reason it's around 22%?
[12:48] Ethan Cole: Two things: prompt variability and session affinity. Your user flows have a lot of single-shot queries with unique IDs, which reduces cache reuse. Also, your current affinity setting routes to any replica; enabling sticky sessions for short conversations could raise hit rate.
[13:06] Priya Singh: Sticky sessions worry us for load balancing fairness.
[13:10] Ethan Cole: Understandable. We can do hybrid: sticky within a short TTL (30s) only for multi-turn flows. That keeps balance and improves KV hit for the right traffic.

[15:00] Maya Chen: Does the team want us to propose an alternative policy that biases latency at peak and cost otherwise? For instance, lower target_latency during business hours and slightly relaxed overnight?
[15:12] Javier Morales: Yes, that's perfect — business-hour strict, off-hour permissive. We'll accept a small increase in tail overnight.

[16:30] Daniel Park: One more ask — can we add a soft quota bump mechanism so that non-critical traffic gracefully degrades to shorter summaries during capacity pressure?
[16:40] Ethan Cole: Absolutely — that's application-level shaping but we have hooks: the router can tag requests as low-priority, and we can route them to a fast summarizer model or truncate max tokens. We'll include example headers and routing rules in the YAML.

[18:50] Priya Singh: What's the rollout plan? We'll want a canary in EU, then global.
[18:58] Maya Chen: Plan: 1) Update autoscale YAML and fallback policy (Redwood sends) 2) Canary in EU with 10% traffic for 24h, run synthetic and real traffic 3) Expand to global if metrics look good. We'll include rollback flags.

[21:20] Javier Morales: Any gotchas we should watch for in the canary?
[21:24] Ethan Cole: Watch KV hit, latency p95, and anomaly rate for hallucination or truncation artifacts when using fallback models. Also keep an eye on cost delta. We'll provide a dashboard widget.

[23:00] Maya Chen: Alright — let's detail action items. (brief pause)

[23:12] Ethan Cole: Quick note — we also recommend a scheduled cache priming job 10 minutes before the expected spike to pre-populate prefix cache if you have predictable endpoints. That reduces the 1st-token penalty.
[23:30] Priya Singh: We'll try that. Any thoughts on observability retention? We need 90 days for audit.
[23:37] Maya Chen: We can enable extended retention as an add-on. I'll include pricing.

[26:15] Daniel Park: Security review follow-up — I want to loop in compliance for the SOC2 logs integration.
[26:24] Maya Chen: We'll schedule a separate 30-minute sync next week.

[28:40] Javier Morales: For the prewarm rehearsal we need an exact load script. Can Redwood provide k6 or locust scripts?
[28:48] Ethan Cole: Yes, we'll share a k6 script tuned to your QPS/token profile, plus a synthetic dataset.

[31:00] Priya Singh: Small nit — the telemetry IDs in the traces you sent had a couple of mangled fields, might be an ingestion mapping problem.
[31:08] Ethan Cole: Thanks, we'll check the ingestion pipeline and the mapping for session_id and request_id.

[34:20] Maya Chen: Okay let's recap next steps — I'll send the YAML and runbook, Ethan stands up fallback variant, Priya runs prewarm rehearsal, Javier shares token distribution.
[34:35] Daniel Park: Sounds good.

[36:00] Maya Chen: Anything else?
[36:04] Priya Singh: No, thanks — timeline looks fine.
[36:07] Javier Morales: One more question: if the fallback model is used, do logs clearly show which model responded? We need end-to-end traceability.
[36:15] Ethan Cole: Yes, every response includes model_id and runtime flags in the audit log. We'll make sure your retention policy includes that field.

[38:00] Maya Chen: Great, we'll follow up via email with the artifacts. Thanks everyone.
[38:07] Daniel Park: Thanks.
[38:09] Priya Singh: Thanks.
[38:10] Javier Morales: Thanks all.

Notes: small transcription glitches present, some acronyms may be mis-heard (KV, KMS). Artifacts referenced: Link: https://redwood.ai/pilot/orion/benchmarks (shared), k6 script and YAML (to be attached).

End of transcript.
